headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Anaemia
headings.content: Anaemia is a pathological condition characterized by a reduction in the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, resulting from a decrease in the concentration of haemoglobin, red blood cell count, or packed cell volume below normal physiological levels. Understanding its pathophysiology is crucial for nursing students, as it underpins every symptom and intervention seen in clinical practice. Under normal circumstances, erythrocytes are produced in the bone marrow through erythropoiesis, stimulated by the hormone erythropoietin released by the kidneys in response to tissue hypoxia. When this delicate balance is disrupted either by accelerated destruction of red blood cells, excessive blood loss, or impaired erythrocyte production, the body experiences systemic oxygen deprivation. To compensate for this hypoxaemia, the cardiovascular system increases cardiac output and respiratory rate, attempting to deliver more oxygen to vital organs. Chronic hypoxia can eventually lead to high-output heart failure if left unaddressed. In the Nigerian context, healthcare professionals frequently encounter anaemia precipitated by nutritional deficiencies, parasitic infections like malaria, and haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease. Recognizing these underlying mechanisms enables nurses to anticipate complications, interpret laboratory findings accurately, and provide holistic, evidence-based care to patients suffering from tissue hypoxia.

headings.title: Classification and Etiology of Anaemia
headings.content: Classifying anaemia effectively allows nurses and clinicians to determine the precise underlying etiology and formulate targeted treatment regimens. Broadly, anaemia is classified based on red blood cell morphology using indices such as the Mean Corpuscular Volume, and by the underlying pathophysiological mechanism, which includes blood loss, decreased production, or increased destruction of erythrocytes. Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia is typically caused by iron deficiency, thalassemia, or lead poisoning, with iron deficiency being exceedingly common in developing countries due to poor dietary intake, chronic blood loss from heavy menstruation, or hookworm infestation. Normocytic, normochromic anaemia often results from acute blood loss, chronic disease states, or early-stage aplastic anaemia, where erythrocytes are normal in size and haemoglobin content but insufficient in number. Conversely, macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia features abnormally large red blood cells and is primarily driven by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) or folate deficiency. Haemolytic anaemia represents a distinct category where red blood cells are prematurely destroyed, which can be inherited, as seen in sickle cell anaemia and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, or acquired through autoimmune responses or infections like malaria. By categorizing anaemia accurately, nursing professionals can better comprehend diagnostic reports and educate patients regarding specific dietary modifications or medical therapies required to correct their specific type of anaemia.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment Findings
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of anaemia depend heavily on the severity of the condition, the speed of its onset, and the patient's baseline cardiopulmonary health. Because reduced haemoglobin diminishes oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues, patients commonly present with generalized fatigue, weakness, pallor of the skin, conjunctiva, nail beds, and palmar creases. Cardiovascular and respiratory signs often manifest as compensatory mechanisms, including tachycardia, palpitations, exertional dyspnoea, and tachypnoea as the body attempts to compensate for tissue hypoxia. In severe or chronic cases, patients may experience neurological symptoms such as headache, dizziness, vertigo, and difficulty concentrating, while angular cheilitis, glossitis, and brittle or spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) are classic physical findings specifically associated with iron deficiency anaemia. Pica, an unusual craving for non-nutritive substances like ice, dirt, or clay, is another notable indicator frequently observed in iron-deficient patients. Comprehensive nursing assessment involves a thorough physical examination, a detailed dietary and medical history, and careful observation of vital signs. Recognizing these clinical findings promptly enables nursing students to identify deteriorating patients early, communicate effectively with the multidisciplinary healthcare team, and implement appropriate supportive nursing measures to ensure patient safety and comfort.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations and Laboratory Evaluations
headings.content: Accurately diagnosing anaemia and identifying its precise etiology requires a systematic approach utilizing various laboratory investigations and diagnostic evaluations. The foundational test is a complete blood count, which measures hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, total red blood cell count, and red blood cell indices including mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration. A peripheral blood smear is frequently performed to visually evaluate the size, shape, color, and structural characteristics of erythrocytes, helping to identify abnormalities such as sickle cells, spherocytes, or schistocytes. To pinpoint specific nutritional deficiencies, healthcare providers order iron profiles—including serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation, and serum ferritin levels—alongside serum vitamin B12 and folate assays. In cases of suspected chronic blood loss or gastrointestinal pathology, stool occult blood tests, endoscopy, or colonoscopy may be indicated. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are reserved for complex cases where bone marrow failure, malignancy, or unexplained cytopenias are suspected. For nursing students, understanding these diagnostic modalities ensures the ability to prepare patients physically and psychologically, interpret laboratory values correctly, and monitor treatment efficacy over time.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of anaemia is directed at correcting the root cause, replenishing depleted nutrient stores, and alleviating tissue hypoxia. For iron deficiency anaemia, oral iron supplementation, such as ferrous sulfate or ferrous gluconate, is the first-line therapy, though parenteral iron preparations like intravenous iron sucrose may be administered if patients experience severe gastrointestinal side effects or have malabsorption syndromes. Vitamin B12 injections (cyanocobalamin) are essential for managing megaloblastic anaemia caused by pernicious anaemia or malabsorption, while oral folic acid supplementation is prescribed for folate-deficiency states. In cases of severe, symptomatic anaemia where hemoglobin levels drop precipitously—such as acute haemorrhage, severe malaria-induced anaemia, or pre-operative optimization—blood transfusions using packed red blood cells are life-saving interventions. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, such as recombinant human erythropoietin, are utilized in patients with chronic kidney disease to stimulate bone marrow red blood cell production. Nurses play a vital role in administering these pharmacological agents safely, monitoring for adverse drug reactions, educating patients on potential side effects like dark stools or gastrointestinal upset from oral iron, and closely observing transfusion recipients for acute transfusion reactions.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Interventions
headings.content: A comprehensive nursing care plan for a patient with anaemia focuses on managing fatigue, ensuring patient safety, optimizing tissue perfusion, and promoting nutritional compliance. Because generalized weakness and fatigue are debilitating, the nurse must prioritize energy conservation techniques, assisting patients with activities of daily living while encouraging a balance between periods of rest and activity. To promote tissue perfusion, vital signs should be monitored regularly, and supplemental oxygen administered if hypoxia is present. Nursing interventions also encompass nutritional counseling, emphasizing the consumption of iron-rich foods, vitamin C to enhance iron absorption, and green leafy vegetables containing folic acid. When administering oral iron, nurses should instruct patients to take it between meals if tolerated, or use a straw if liquid supplements are prescribed to prevent dental staining. Safety precautions are paramount, especially for elderly or severely weak patients who are at risk for orthostatic hypotension and falls; thus, assistance with ambulation and gradual position changes must be enforced. Documenting patient responses to interventions and regularly reassessing hemoglobin levels ensure that the nursing care plan remains dynamic and responsive to the patient's clinical progress.

headings.title: Complications and Patient Education in Anaemia
headings.content: Recognizing potential complications and providing thorough patient education are critical final components of holistic anaemia care. Untreated or chronic severe anaemia can lead to serious complications, including high-output cardiac failure, angina, cardiomegaly, increased susceptibility to severe infections, and developmental delays in growing children. In pregnant women, severe anaemia poses grave risks, such as postpartum hemorrhage, low birth weight, premature delivery, and increased maternal mortality. Patient education must be tailored to the local cultural and socioeconomic context, focusing on dietary modifications, adherence to prescribed medications, and the importance of identifying and treating underlying causes like malaria or worm infestations. Nurses must educate patients on recognizing warning signs of worsening anaemia—such as extreme shortness of breath, chest pain, severe dizziness, or fainting—and knowing when to seek immediate medical attention. Emphasizing regular follow-up clinic visits and routine hemoglobin checks empowers patients and their families to take an active role in their health management, preventing relapse and promoting long-term wellness.
